metadata.title: Cocliques in the Kneser graph on (n-1,n)-flags of PG(2n,q)

nodes.name: $i$-space
nodes.statement: An \emph{$i$-space} of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$ is a subspace of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$ with projective dimension $i$, in particular a $0$-space is a point, a $1$-space is a line and so on.

nodes.name: $(n-1,n)$-flag
nodes.statement: Now, consider an $(n-1)$-space $A$ and an $n$-space $B$ of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$. If $A$ is contained in $B$, we call $(A,B)$ an \emph{$(n-1,n)$-flag} of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$.
nodes.statement_short: A pair $(A,B)$ of an $(n-1)$-space contained in an $n$-space.

nodes.name: Opposite flags
nodes.statement: Two such flags $(A_1,B_1)$ and $(A_2,B_2)$ are called \emph{opposite} if $A_1\cap B_2=A_2\cap B_1=\emptyset$.

nodes.name: Kneser graph $\Gamma_{2n}$ on $(n-1,n)$-flags
nodes.statement: For $n\geq 2$ let $\Gamma_{2n}$ be the graph whose vertices are the $(n-1,n)$-flags of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$, with two vertices being adjacent if the corresponding flags are opposite.
differentia: two vertices being adjacent if the corresponding flags are opposite
nodes.statement_short: Graph on $(n-1,n)$-flags of PG$(2n,q)$, adjacency = opposition.

nodes.name: Large cocliques of $\Gamma_{2n}$ (hyperplane/point constructions)
nodes.statement:
\begin{enumerate} [(a)]
    \item Let $H$ be a hyperplane of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$ and let $X$ be either $(i)$ a point of $H$, or $(ii)$ an $(2n-2)$-space incident with $H$.
    Now, let $\mathcal{F}$ be the set of all $(n-1,n)$-flags such that for every $(A,B)\in \mathcal{F}$ we have $B\subseteq H$, or $A$ is incident with $X$ and $H$.
    \item Let $P$ be a point of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$ and let $X$ be either $(i)$ a hyperplane incident with $P$, or $(ii)$ a line incident with $P$.
    Now, let $\mathcal{F}$ be the set of all $(n-1,n)$-flags such that for every $(A,B)\in \mathcal{F}$ we have $P\subseteq A$, or $B$ is incident with $X$ and $P$.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Two dual families of cocliques: flags with $B$ in a hyperplane $H$ or $A$ through $X$ and $H$; dually flags with $A$ through a point $P$ or $B$ through $X$ and $P$.
nodes.label: E: main

nodes.name: Blokhuis-Brouwer Theorem 5.1 (Example 1.1 is a coclique)
nodes.statement: It was already observed in Theorem 5.1 of \cite{cocliquesonlineplane4d} that the construction of Example \ref{E: main} does not contain opposite flags, i.e. the construction yields a coclique of $\Gamma_{2n}$.
conclusions: the construction yields a coclique of $\Gamma_{2n}$
nodes.statement_short: The constructions of Example 1.1 contain no opposite flags.

nodes.name: Duality of the constructions
nodes.statement:
Observe that parts (a) and (b) of \Cref{E: main} are dual to one another.
There is also some form of duality between the parts $(i)$ and $(ii)$. Consider for example case $(a)$, then $X$ is either a point or a hyperplane of $H$.
nodes.statement_short: Parts (a)/(b) of Example 1.1 are dual; parts (i)/(ii) are related by duality inside $H$.

nodes.name: Gaussian coefficient
nodes.statement_short: The $q$-binomial coefficient $\prod_{i=1}^a (q^{b-a+i}-1)/(q^i-1)$ for $0\le a\le b$, else $0$.

nodes.name: Degree of the Gaussian coefficient
nodes.statement: The term $\Gauss{b}{a}$ is a $q$-polynomial of degree $a(b-a)$, so in particular $\Gauss{b}{a}$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{a(b-a)})$.
conclusions: $\Gauss{b}{a}$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{a(b-a)})$
is a $q$-polynomial of degree $a(b-a)$

nodes.name: Count of the construction in Example 1.1 (a)(i)
nodes.statement:
Now, we count the size of the set $\mathcal{F}$ as described in \Cref{E: main} $(a)(i)$ and remark that duality implies that all constructions described in \Cref{E: main} have the same size.

The number of $n$-spaces incident with a hyperplane $H$ of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$ is $\Gauss{2n}{n+1}$. Each such $n$-space contains exactly $\Gauss{n+1}{1}$ many $(n-1)$-spaces. The number of $(n-1)$-spaces incident with the point $X$ and the hyperplane $H$ is $\Gauss{2n-1}{n-1}$. Each such $(n-1)$-space is incident with exactly $q^n$ many $n$-spaces that are not contained in $H$.
nodes.statement_short: Direct double count: flags with $B\subseteq H$, plus flags with $A$ through $X$ in $H$ and $B\not\subseteq H$.

nodes.name: Size of the constructions of Example 1.1
nodes.statement: Thus the set in question has size $\Gauss{2n}{n+1} \Gauss{n+1}{1} +\Gauss{2n-1}{n-1}q^n$.
conclusions: the set in question has size $\Gauss{2n}{n+1} \Gauss{n+1}{1} +\Gauss{2n-1}{n-1}q^n$

nodes.name: $f(n,q)$
nodes.statement_short: $f(n,q)$ is the Hilton-Milner-type bound: $3[n]_q[2n-2,n-2]_q$ for $n,q\ge4$, and an explicit degree-5 polynomial for $n=3$.

nodes.name: Classification of maximal cocliques of $\Gamma_{2n}$
nodes.statement:
For $n\geq 3$ let $\Gamma_{2n}$ be the graph whose vertices are the $(n-1,n)$-flags of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$, with two vertices being adjacent if the corresponding flags are opposite. For $q$ large enough compared to $n$, a maximal coclique $\mathcal{F}$ of $\Gamma_{2n}$ falls into exactly one of the following categories.
\begin{enumerate} [(a)]
    \item $|\mathcal{F}|=\Gauss{2n}{n-1} \Gauss{n+1}{1} +\Gauss{2n-1}{n-1}q^n$ and $\mathcal{F}$ is one of the structures described in Example \ref{E: main}.
    \item $|\mathcal{F}|\leq \Gauss{2n}{n-1} \Gauss{n+1}{1} +f(n,q)\cdot q^n$ and there is either a hyperplane $H$, such that $\mathcal{F}$ contains all flags $(A,B)$ with $B\subseteq H$, or there is a point $P$ such that $\mathcal{F}$ contains all flags $(A,B)$ with $P\subseteq A$.
    \item $|\mathcal{F}|$ is at most $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2+n-2})$.
\end{enumerate}
assumptions: For $n\geq 3$ let $\Gamma_{2n}$ be the graph whose vertices are the $(n-1,n)$-flags of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$, with two vertices being adjacent if the corresponding flags are opposite.
For $q$ large enough compared to $n$
conclusions: a maximal coclique $\mathcal{F}$ of $\Gamma_{2n}$ falls into exactly one of the following categories.
nodes.statement_short: For large $q$, a maximal coclique of $\Gamma_{2n}$ is an Example 1.1 construction, or contains all flags in a hyperplane/through a point with a smaller size bound, or has size $O(q^{n^2+n-2})$.
nodes.label: T: main

nodes.name: $f(n,q)$ is smaller than $\Gauss{2n-1}{n-1}$
nodes.statement: It is quickly checked that $f(n,q)<\Gauss{2n-1}{n-1}$ for large $q$, as $\Gauss{2n-1}{n-1}$ is a $q$-polynomial of degree $(n-1)n$, whereas $f(n,q)$ is a $q$-polynomial of degree $(n-1)+(n-2)n=(n-1)n-1$.
nodes.statement_short: Degree comparison shows $f(n,q)$ is below $[2n-1,n-1]_q$ for large $q$, so case (b) is smaller than case (a).

nodes.name: Case $n=3$ of the main theorem
nodes.statement: For $n=3$ the theorem follows from \cite{werner_metsch}.

nodes.name: Proof of the chromatic number corollary
nodes.statement: In 2023 the chromatic number of $\Gamma_{2n}$ was determined modulo a conjecture by D'haeseleer, Metsch and Werner \cite{Jozefien_some}. Theorem \ref{T: main} is precisely the confirmation that their conjecture is true. Therefore, by proving Theorem \ref{T: main} we immediately get the following.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 1.2 confirms the conjecture of D'haeseleer, Metsch and Werner, on which their chromatic number result depends.

nodes.name: Chromatic number of $\Gamma_{2n}$
nodes.statement: For $q$ large enough, the chromatic number of $\Gamma_{2n}$ is $\frac{q^{n+2}-1}{q-1}-q$.
assumptions: For $q$ large enough
conclusions: the chromatic number of $\Gamma_{2n}$ is $\frac{q^{n+2}-1}{q-1}-q$

nodes.name: $\mathcal{F}$ (a maximal coclique)
nodes.statement: Throughout this paper, we will denote by $\mathcal{F}$ a maximal coclique of $\Gamma_{2n}$.

nodes.name: Possible weights of $n$-spaces
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a maximal coclique of $\Gamma_{2n}$.
    Let $B$ be an $n$-space of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$ that occurs in a flag of $\mathcal{F}$. There exists a $k\in\{1,\ldots,n+1\}$, such that the number of flags in $\mathcal{F}$ that contain $B$ is precisely $\Gauss{k}{1}$. Furthermore, the number in question is $\Gauss{n+1}{1}$ if and only if every flag $(A',B')\in \mathcal{F}$ satisfies $A'\cap B\neq \emptyset$.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a maximal coclique of $\Gamma_{2n}$.
Let $B$ be an $n$-space of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$ that occurs in a flag of $\mathcal{F}$.
conclusions: There exists a $k\in\{1,\ldots,n+1\}$, such that the number of flags in $\mathcal{F}$ that contain $B$ is precisely $\Gauss{k}{1}$.
the number in question is $\Gauss{n+1}{1}$ if and only if every flag $(A',B')\in \mathcal{F}$ satisfies $A'\cap B\neq \emptyset$.
nodes.statement_short: The number of flags of $\mathcal{F}$ through an $n$-space $B$ is a Gaussian $[k]_q$, and is maximal iff every $A'$ of $\mathcal{F}$ meets $B$.
nodes.label: L: possible weights

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.1
nodes.statement:
First, assume that the number  of flags in $\mathcal{F}$ that contain $B$ is $\Gauss{n+1}{1}$. This means that for every $(n-1)$-space $A$ contained in $B$, we have $(A,B)\in \mathcal{F}$. Let $(A',B')$ be an $(n-1,n)$-flag of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$ with $A'\cap B=\emptyset$. Then $B\cap B'$ is just a point $P$. There exist $(n-1)$-spaces in $B$ that are skew to $P$. Therefore, there are flags in $\mathcal{F}$ that are opposite to $(A',B')$, hence $(A',B')$ is not in $\mathcal{F}$.

    Now, assume that every flag $(A',B')\in \mathcal{F}$ satisfies $A'\cap B\neq \emptyset$. Then every flag $(A,B)$, where $A$ is an $(n-1)$-space contained in $B$, is non-opposite to all flags in $\mathcal{F}$. By maximality of $\mathcal{F}$, all such flags are in $\mathcal{F}$. The number of flags in $\mathcal{F}$ containing $B$ is $\Gauss{n+1}{n}=\Gauss{n+1}{1}$.

    Finally, assume that there exist $(n-1,n)$-flags in $\mathcal{F}$ whose $(n-1)$-spaces are skew to $B$. Let $(A'_1,B'_1),\ldots,(A'_k,B'_k)$ be all these flags. Now, any flag $(A,B)\in \mathcal{F}$ has to satisfy $A\cap B'_1\neq\emptyset,\ldots, A\cap B'_k\neq\emptyset$. 
    Let $1\leq i\leq k$.
    As $A'_i\cap B=\emptyset$, we know that $B'_i\cap B$ is a point, say $P_i$.
    Now $A$ has to be incident with all points $P_i$. In other words, the span of the points $P_i$ has to be incident with $A$. Let $s$ be the dimension of the span $S$ of the points $P_i$.
    We have $0\leq s\leq n-1$, otherwise there could be no flag in $\mathcal{F}$ that contains $B$. 
    By maximality of $\mathcal{F}$, any $(n-1)$-space $A$ that is incident with $S$ and $B$ occurs in a flag $(A,B)$ of $\mathcal{F}$. There are $\Gauss{n-s}{(n-1)-s}=\Gauss{n-s}{1}$ such flags.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on whether some flag of $\mathcal{F}$ has $A'$ skew to $B$; maximality forces all $(n-1)$-spaces of $B$ through the span $S$ of the points $B'_i\cap B$.

nodes.name: $\mathcal{F}$-red and $\mathcal{F}$-yellow spaces
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a maximal coclique of $\Gamma_{2n}$.
    An $n$-space $B$, or an $(n-1)$-space $A$ that occurs in $\Gauss{n+1}{1}$ flags of $\mathcal{F}$ is called $\mathcal{F}$-red or, if there is no risk of confusion, simply red. If the space in question occurs only in $\leq \Gauss{n}{1}$ flags of $\mathcal{F}$, but at least in $1$, we call it $\mathcal{F}$-yellow or, if there is no risk of confusion, simply yellow.
nodes.statement_short: A space is red if it lies in the maximum number $[n+1]_q$ of flags of $\mathcal{F}$, yellow if in between $1$ and $[n]_q$.

nodes.name: General position of $(n-1)$-spaces
nodes.statement: Two $(n-1)$-spaces of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$ are in general position if they do not intersect.

nodes.name: General position of $n$-spaces
nodes.statement: Dually, two $n$-spaces of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$ are in general position if they span the entire space and hence intersect only in a point.

nodes.name: Non-general-position $n$-spaces meet in a line
nodes.statement: Therefore, two $n$-spaces of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$ that are not in general position intersect in at least a line.
assumptions: two $n$-spaces of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$ that are not in general position
conclusions: intersect in at least a line

nodes.name: Red spaces pairwise meet
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a maximal coclique of $\Gamma_{2n}$.
Any two red $(n-1)$-spaces always meet.
Any two red $n$-spaces are not in general position.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a maximal coclique of $\Gamma_{2n}$.
conclusions: Any two red $(n-1)$-spaces always meet.
Any two red $n$-spaces are not in general position.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.4
nodes.statement:
We only show the statement regarding $n$-spaces, the statement for $(n-1)$-spaces follows by duality.

By Lemma \ref{L: possible weights} an $n$-space $B$ is red if and only if every flag $(A',B')\in \mathcal{F}$ satisfies $A'\cap B\neq \emptyset$. If $B_1$ and $B_2$ are two $n$-spaces in general position, i.e. they intersect only in a point, then there exist $(n-1)$-spaces $A_1, A_2$ with $A_1\subseteq B_1$ and $A_2\subseteq B_2$, such that  $A_1\cap B_2=A_2\cap B_1=\emptyset$.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 2.1 red means every $A'$ meets $B$; two $n$-spaces in general position contain skew $(n-1)$-spaces giving opposite flags. Dual for $(n-1)$-spaces.

nodes.name: EKR and Hilton-Milner Theorem for vector spaces
nodes.statement:
(\cite{hiltonmilner_vectorspaces, ekr_vectorspaces}) Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a set of pairwise intersecting $(n-1)$-spaces of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$, with $n\geq 3$ and $q\geq 3$.
Then either $|\mathcal{C}|\leq \Gauss{2n}{n-1}-q^{n(n-1)}\Gauss{n}{1}$, or there exists a point $P$, such that every $(n-1)$-space is incident with $P$.
nodes.origin_citation: Hilton-Milner for vector spaces; EKR for vector spaces
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a set of pairwise intersecting $(n-1)$-spaces of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$, with $n\geq 3$ and $q\geq 3$.
conclusions: either $|\mathcal{C}|\leq \Gauss{2n}{n-1}-q^{n(n-1)}\Gauss{n}{1}$, or there exists a point $P$, such that every $(n-1)$-space is incident with $P$.
nodes.statement_short: An intersecting family of $(n-1)$-spaces in PG$(2n,q)$ is either small (Hilton-Milner bound) or a point-pencil.
nodes.label: R: EKR + HM vectorspaces

nodes.name: Degree of the Hilton-Milner bound
nodes.statement: We remark that $\Gauss{2n}{n-1}-q^{n(n-1)}\Gauss{n}{1}$ is a polynomial in $q$ of degree at most $n^2-2$.
nodes.label: Remark 1

nodes.name: Number of red spaces
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a maximal coclique of $\Gamma_{2n}$ with $n\geq 3$.
Either the number of red $(n-1)$-spaces in $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-2})$, or there is a point $P$ and every $(n-1)$-space incident with $P$ is red.\\
Either the number of red $n$-spaces in $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-2})$, or there is a hyperplane $H$ and every $n$-space incident with $H$ is red.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a maximal coclique of $\Gamma_{2n}$ with $n\geq 3$.
conclusions: Either the number of red $(n-1)$-spaces in $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-2})$, or there is a point $P$ and every $(n-1)$-space incident with $P$ is red.
Either the number of red $n$-spaces in $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-2})$, or there is a hyperplane $H$ and every $n$-space incident with $H$ is red.
nodes.statement_short: Either few ($O(q^{n^2-2})$) red spaces, or all $(n-1)$-spaces through a point (dually all $n$-spaces in a hyperplane) are red.
nodes.label: C: number of red spaces

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.7
nodes.statement:
Assume that the number of red $(n-1)$-spaces in $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$ is not $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-2})$, then it is in particular $> \Gauss{2n}{n-1}-q^{n(n-1)}\Gauss{n}{1}$ for $n\geq 3$. \Cref{R: EKR + HM vectorspaces} and \Cref{Remark 1} imply that there exists a point $P$, such that every red $(n-1)$-space is incident with $P$. 

    By \Cref{C: possible weights}, for every flag $(A,B)\in \mathcal{F}$, we have that it's $n$-space meets all red $(n-1)$-spaces.
    Let $B$ be an $n$-space that intersects all red $(n-1)$-spaces with $P\notin B$. The number of lines that meet $P$ and $B$ is $\Gauss{n+1}{1}$, as this is the number of points in $B$. The number of $(n-1)$-subspaces incident with a line is $\Gauss{2n-1}{n-2}$. Therefore, there are at most $\Gauss{n+1}{1}\cdot \Gauss{2n-1}{n-2}$ red $(n-1)$-spaces in this case and this number is $\mathcal{O}(q^n)\cdot \mathcal{O}(q^{(n-2)(n+1)})=\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-2})$, a contradiction.

Hence, for all flags $(A,B)\in \mathcal{F}$, it's $n$-space meets $P$. By maximality of $\mathcal{F}$, every $(n-1)$-space incident with $P$ is red. For $n$-spaces the statement follows by duality.
nodes.statement_short: Many red $(n-1)$-spaces force a common point $P$ by EKR/Hilton-Milner; an $n$-space missing $P$ would meet too few red spaces, contradiction; maximality concludes.

nodes.name: EKR and Hilton-Milner Theorem for $(n-1)$-spaces of $\mathrm{PG}(2n-1,q)$
nodes.origin_citation: Newman PhD thesis Thm 5.3.1; Ihringer (Hilton-Milner) Thm 6; Thm 6.1 of the k=3 Hilton-Milner paper
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a set of pairwise intersecting $(n-1)$-spaces of $\mathrm{PG}(2n-1,q)$.
conclusions: Then there exists a point or hyperplane in $\mathrm{PG}(2n-1,q)$ that is incident with all $(n-1)$-spaces. In particular, $|\mathcal{C}|=\Gauss{2n-1}{n-1}$.
Then $|\mathcal{C}|<3\Gauss{n}{1}\Gauss{2n-2}{n-2}$.
Then $|\mathcal{C}|\leq q^5+2q^4+3q^3+2q^2+q+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Largest intersecting families of $(n-1)$-spaces in PG$(2n-1,q)$ are point or hyperplane stars; otherwise the Hilton-Milner bounds hold.
nodes.label: R: EKR for n=2k

nodes.name: Many red $n$-spaces
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a maximal coclique of $\Gamma_{2n}$ with $n\geq 3$ in which the number of red $n$-spaces is not $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-2})$. Then $\mathcal{F}$ is as in Example \ref{E: main} (a), or $|\mathcal{F}|\leq  \Gauss{2n}{n-1} \Gauss{n+1}{1} +f(n,q)\cdot q^n $ and there is a hyperplane $H$, such that $\mathcal{F}$ contains all flags $(A,B)$ with $B\subseteq H$.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a maximal coclique of $\Gamma_{2n}$ with $n\geq 3$ in which the number of red $n$-spaces is not $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-2})$.
conclusions: Then $\mathcal{F}$ is as in Example \ref{E: main} (a), or $|\mathcal{F}|\leq  \Gauss{2n}{n-1} \Gauss{n+1}{1} +f(n,q)\cdot q^n $ and there is a hyperplane $H$, such that $\mathcal{F}$ contains all flags $(A,B)$ with $B\subseteq H$.
nodes.statement_short: With many red $n$-spaces, $\mathcal{F}$ is Example 1.1(a) or contains all flags in a hyperplane and has size at most $[2n,n-1][n+1]+f(n,q)q^n$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.2
nodes.statement:
By \Cref{C: number of red spaces}, we know that there is a hyperplane $H$ such that every $n$-space incident with $H$ is red. By \Cref{L: possible weights}, we have for any flag $(A,B)$ in $\mathcal{F}$ that $A$ intersects all the $n$-spaces in $H$. This is only possible if $A\subseteq H$. The number of flags $(A,B)$ with $A,B\subseteq H$ is $\Gauss{2n}{n+1} \Gauss{n+1}{n}=\Gauss{2n}{n-1} \Gauss{n+1}{1}$.

    Let $(A_1,B_1)$ and $(A_2,B_2)$ be flags of $\mathcal{F}$ with $B_1,B_2$ not red, i.e. $B_1,B_2$ are not contained in $H$. If $A_1$ and $A_2$ are skew, then $B_1$ is skew to $A_2$, as $B_1$ intersects $H$ only in $A_1$. Similarly $B_2$ is skew to $A_1$. So if $A_1$ and $A_2$ are skew, then the flags $(A_1,B_1)$ and $(A_2,B_2)$ are opposite, which is a contradiction. 

    In conclusion the flags $(A,B)$ in $\mathcal{F}$ with $B\not\subseteq H$ have $(n-1)$-spaces that pairwise intersect in $H$. By \Cref{R: EKR for n=2k} there are two options. Either there is a point or $(2n-2)$-space in $H$ that is incident with $A$ for any such flag $(A,B)$, or there are at most $f(n,q)$ distinct $(n-1)$-subspaces $A$ in these flags. 
    If there is a point or $(2n-2)$-space in $H$ that is incident with $A$ for any flag $(A,B)$ with $B\not\subseteq H$, then $\mathcal{F}$ is as in Example \ref{E: main} (a).
    If no such point or $(2n-2)$-space exists, then we have $ \Gauss{2n}{n-1} \Gauss{n+1}{1}$ flags $(A,B)$ with $A,B\subseteq H$ and since any $(n-1)$-space in $H$ is incident with $q^n$ many $n$-spaces that are not contained in $H$, we have at most $q^n\cdot f(n,q)$ many flags $(A,B)$ with $B\not\subseteq H$. In conclusion, we have at most $\Gauss{2n}{n-1} \Gauss{n+1}{1} +f(n,q)\cdot q^n$ flags in this case.
nodes.statement_short: All $n$-spaces of a hyperplane $H$ are red, forcing $A\subseteq H$; the $A$'s of flags outside $H$ pairwise meet, so EKR/Hilton-Milner in $H$ gives Example 1.1(a) or the $f(n,q)$ bound.

nodes.name: Erd\H{o}s-Matching Theorem for vector spaces
nodes.statement: (\cite{Ihringer_EM}) Let $n\geq 3$ and let $\mathcal{C}$ be a family of $(n-1)$-spaces in $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$, such that $\mathcal{C}$ does not contain $s+1$ pairwise skew $(n-1)$-spaces. Then $|\mathcal{C}|\leq s \Gauss{2n}{n-1}$, for $q$ large enough compared to $n$.
assumptions: Let $n\geq 3$
let $\mathcal{C}$ be a family of $(n-1)$-spaces in $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$, such that $\mathcal{C}$ does not contain $s+1$ pairwise skew $(n-1)$-spaces.
for $q$ large enough compared to $n$
conclusions: Then $|\mathcal{C}|\leq s \Gauss{2n}{n-1}$
nodes.label: R: EM for vector spaces

nodes.name: Many pairwise skew yellow spaces
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a maximal coclique of $\Gamma_{2n}$ with $n\geq 3$ and assume that the number of red spaces is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-2})$. Then $|\mathcal{F}|$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2+n-2})$, or there are at least $n+1$ yellow $(n-1)$-spaces in $\mathcal{F}$ that are pairwise skew, or there are at least $n+1$ yellow $n$-spaces in general position.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a maximal coclique of $\Gamma_{2n}$ with $n\geq 3$
assume that the number of red spaces is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-2})$.
conclusions: Then $|\mathcal{F}|$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2+n-2})$, or there are at least $n+1$ yellow $(n-1)$-spaces in $\mathcal{F}$ that are pairwise skew, or there are at least $n+1$ yellow $n$-spaces in general position.
nodes.statement_short: With few red spaces, either $|\mathcal{F}|=O(q^{n^2+n-2})$ or there are $n+1$ pairwise skew yellow $(n-1)$-spaces (or dually $n+1$ yellow $n$-spaces in general position).
nodes.label: L: many yellow pw skew

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.2
nodes.statement:
The number of red spaces is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-2})$ and a red space is contained in $\Gauss{n+1}{1}$ flags of $\mathcal{F}$, hence the number of flags in $\mathcal{F}$ that contain a red space is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-2})\cdot \Gauss{n+1}{1}=\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2+n-2})$. 

    Let us assume that $|\mathcal{F}|$ is not $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2+n-2})$. 
    As a yellow space is contained in at most $\Gauss{n}{1}$ flags of $\mathcal{F}$, the number of yellow spaces cannot be $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})$. If there are at most $n$ yellow $(n-1)$-spaces in $\mathcal{F}$ that are pairwise skew, \Cref{R: EM for vector spaces} implies that the number of yellow $(n-1)$-spaces is at most $n \Gauss{2n}{n-1}$ which is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})$. For yellow $n$-spaces the result follows by duality.
nodes.statement_short: Flags on red spaces are few; if $|\mathcal{F}|$ is large there are many yellow spaces, and the Erdős-Matching theorem then yields $n+1$ pairwise skew ones.

nodes.name: Few $n$-spaces meet $n+1$ pairwise skew $(n-1)$-spaces
nodes.statement: Let $A_1,\ldots,A_{n+1}$ be pairwise skew $(n-1)$-spaces of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$. The number of $n$-spaces that intersect every $A_i$ for $1\leq i\leq n+1$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})$.
assumptions: Let $A_1,\ldots,A_{n+1}$ be pairwise skew $(n-1)$-spaces of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$.
conclusions: The number of $n$-spaces that intersect every $A_i$ for $1\leq i\leq n+1$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})$.
nodes.label: L: few that meet all

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.3
nodes.statement:
Let $B$ be an $n$-space that meets $A_1,\ldots,A_{n+1}$. 
     Then $B\cap A_i$ has to be some subspace $P_i$ for all $1\leq i\leq n+1$.

First, we will count subspaces $P_i$ in $A_i$ (for $i$ in a subset of $\{1,\ldots,n+1\}$) and then we will consider all $n$-spaces incident with the span of the $P_i$. This gives an upper bound on the number of $n$-spaces that meet $A_1,\ldots,A_{n+1}$.

As a first step, we can choose dimensions $s_1,\ldots,s_{n+1}$, where $s_i=dim(P_i)$. As $0\leq s_i\leq n-1$, there are $n$ options for every $i$, so in total at most $n^{n+1}$ options. From now on, we assume that $s_1,\ldots,s_{n+1}$ are fixed.


We distinguish two cases: Either we choose $P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1}$ in such a way that there is an $i$, such that the span $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i'} \rangle$ meets $A_{i'+1}$, or we choose $P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1}$ such that there is no such $i'$.


\textbf{\underline{Case 1:}} We choose $P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1}$, such that there exists an $i'\in \{2,\ldots,n\}$, with the property that the span $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i'} \rangle$ meets $A_{i'+1}$. Let $i$ be the smallest integer with this property.\\

This implies that $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$ does not meet $A_i$, hence $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$ is skew to $P_i$. Furthermore, $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-2} \rangle$ does not meet $A_{i-1}$, hence $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-2} \rangle$ is skew to $P_{i-1}$, so $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-2} \rangle$, $P_{i-1}$ and $P_i$ are pairwise skew. Using the same argument $i-1$ times yields that $P_1,\ldots,P_i$ are pairwise skew.

In particular, we have
\begin{align} \begin{split}
    dim(\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i} \rangle)&=dim( P_1)+\ldots+dim(P_i)+(i-1)\\
    &= s_1+\ldots+s_i+(i-1)   
\end{split}
\end{align}
and
\begin{align} dim(\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle)=s_1+\ldots+s_{i-1}+(i-2). 
\end{align}
For any $j\leq i-1$ the number of $s_j$-subspaces in $A_j$ is $\Gauss{n}{s_j+1}$.
 As $P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1}$ are pairwise skew, the number of distinct subspaces $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$ is bound by the number of tuples $( P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1})$. So, the number of subspaces $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$ is at most
 $\Gauss{n}{s_1+1} \ldots   \Gauss{n}{s_{i-1}+1}$.

For any subspace $P_i$ skew to $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$, we have that $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1},P_i \rangle=\langle \langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle,P_i \rangle$ consists of all points that are on a line $g$ that intersects $P_i$ and $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$.\\
 Let $Q_1$ be a point in  $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$. As $Q_1$ is in  $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$, which is skew to the $(n-1)$-space $A_i$, the span $S$ of $Q_1$ and $A_i$ has dimension $n$. If we assume that $S$ meets $A_{i+1}$ in at least a line, then $A_i$ (which has codimension $1$ in $S$) would meet $A_{i+1}$, which is a contradiction. 
 So, $S$ meets $A_{i+1}$ in at most a point $Q_3$. If such a point $Q_3$ exists, then the line $Q_1Q_3$ intersects $P_i$ in a point.
In other words: For every point $Q_1$ in $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$ there is at most one point $Q_2$ in $A_i$ with the property that $Q_1Q_2$ intersects $A_{i+1}$.
 Recall from (\ref{A: dim P_1,...,P_i-1}) that $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1}\rangle$ has dimension $s_1+\ldots+s_{i-1}+(i-2)$.
 Therefore, $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1}\rangle$ contains exactly $\Gauss{s_1+\ldots+s_{i-1}+ (i-1)}{1}$ many points $Q_1$.
Hence, the number of points $Q_2$ in $A_i$, with the property that there is a $Q_1$ in $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1}\rangle$ such that $Q_1Q_2$ intersects $A_{i+1}$, is at most  $\Gauss{s_1+\ldots+s_{i-1}+ (i-1)}{1}$. \\
As $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i} \rangle$ meets $A_{i+1}$, we have that $P_i$ is an $s_i$-subspaces in $A_i$ that is incident with one such point $Q_2$. The number of $s_i$-subspaces in $A_i$ incident with a fixed point is $\Gauss{n-1}{s_i}$.
 So, if $P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1}$ are fixed, there are at most $\Gauss{s_1+\ldots+s_{i-1}+ (i-1)}{1}\Gauss{n-1}{s_i}$ options for $P_i$. \\ 
Recall from (\ref{A: dim P_1,...,P_i}) that $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i} \rangle$ has dimension $(s_1+\ldots+s_i+i-1)$.
Therefore, the number of $n$-spaces $B$ that contain  $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i} \rangle$ is at most
 $\Gauss{2n-(s_1+\ldots+s_i+i-1)}{n-(s_1+\ldots+s_i+i-1)}$.  
Any $n$-space that contains $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1} \rangle$, must also contain $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i} \rangle$. Hence, we have at most
    \begin{align*}
        &\Gauss{n}{s_1+1} \ldots   \Gauss{n}{s_{i-1}+1}  \cdot \Gauss{s_1+\ldots+s_{i-1}+i-1}{1}\Gauss{n-1}{s_i}   \cdot\Gauss{2n-(s_1+\ldots+s_i+i-1)}{n-(s_1+\ldots+s_i+i-1)}
    \end{align*}
   many $n$-subspaces $B$ in Case 1. This number is a $q$-polynomial of degree at most
\begin{align*}
    &\left( \sum\limits_{j=1}^{i-1}(s_j+1)(n-s_j-1) \right)
    +(i-2+\sum\limits_{j=1}^{i-1}s_j)+s_i(n-1-s_i)+(n-i+1-\sum\limits_{j=1}^{i}s_j)n\\
    &=n^2 -\sum\limits_{j=1}^{i}(s_j^2+s_j) - 1\leq n^2-1.
\end{align*}

This implies that in this case the number in question is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})$.\\

\textbf{\underline{Case 2:}} We choose $P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1}$, such that there exists  no $i'\in \{2,\ldots,n\}$, with the property that the span $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i'} \rangle$ meets $A_{i'+1}$. \\

We start with the same argument as in Case 1. 
The span $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{n} \rangle$ does not meet $A_{n+1}$, hence $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{n} \rangle$ is skew to $P_{n+1}$. 
Furthermore, $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{n-1} \rangle$ does not meet $A_{n}$, hence $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{n-1} \rangle$ is skew to $P_{n}$, so $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{n-1} \rangle$, $P_{n}$ and $P_{n+1}$ are pairwise skew. 
Using the same argument $n$ times yields that $P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1}$ are pairwise skew. Hence, 
$\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1}\rangle$ has dimension $s_1+\ldots+s_{n+1}+n$.\\
Let $B$ be an $n$-space that contains $P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1}$.
As $B$ has dimension $n$, we have $s_1+\ldots+s_{n+1}+n\leq n$, hence $s_i=0$ for all $1\leq i\leq n+1$ and every subspace $P_i$ is a point. In particular, $B$ is the span of all points $P_i$. There are $\Gauss{n}{1}$ points in every $(n-1)$-space $A_i$, hence there are at most $\Gauss{n}{1}^{n+1}$ many $n$-spaces $B$ that are equal to $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1} \rangle$ and this number is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})$.\\

In conclusion we see that in both cases the number in question is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix the dimensions of $P_i=B\cap A_i$ and split by whether some partial span $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i'}\rangle$ meets $A_{i'+1}$. In Case 1 bound the choices of $P_i$ via points $Q_2$ and compute a $q$-degree $\le n^2-1$; in Case 2 all $P_i$ are points spanning $B$.

nodes.name: Dimension of $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_i\rangle$
nodes.label: A: dim P_1,...,P_i

nodes.name: Dimension of $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1}\rangle$
nodes.statement: dim(\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle)=s_1+\ldots+s_{i-1}+(i-2).
nodes.label: A: dim P_1,...,P_i-1

nodes.name: Yellow $n$-spaces meet almost all flags
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a maximal coclique of $\Gamma_{2n}$ with $n\geq 3$ and let $B$ be a yellow $n$-space of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$. The number of flags $(A',B')\in \mathcal{F}$ with pairwise distinct $n$-spaces and with $A'\cap B=\emptyset$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})$.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a maximal coclique of $\Gamma_{2n}$ with $n\geq 3$
let $B$ be a yellow $n$-space of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$.
conclusions: The number of flags $(A',B')\in \mathcal{F}$ with pairwise distinct $n$-spaces and with $A'\cap B=\emptyset$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})$.
nodes.label: L: yellows meet almost all

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.4
nodes.statement:
Since $B$ is a yellow $n$-space there exists an $(n-1)$-space $A$, such that $(A,B)\in \mathcal{F}$. Therefore, any flag $(A',B')\in \mathcal{F}$ with $A'\cap B=\emptyset$ has to satisfy that the point $B'\cap B$ is in  $A$. 

    Consider two flags $(A'_1,B'_1),(A'_2,B'_2)\in \mathcal{F}$ with $A'_1\cap B=\emptyset$ and $A'_2\cap B=\emptyset$ and assume $B'_1\cap B=B'_2\cap B=P$.
    If $B'_1\cap B'_2=P$, then $A'_1\cap B'_2=\emptyset=A'_2\cap B'_1$ as $A'_1$ and $A'_2$ are skew to $B$. Then the flags $(A'_1,B'_1),(A'_2,B'_2)$ are opposite, which is a contradiction. Therefore, the $n$-spaces $B'_1$ and $B'_2$ have to meet in at least a line containing $P$.
    In the quotient space of $P$, which has dimension $2n-1$, this means that the $(n-1)$-spaces corresponding to $B'_1$ and $B'_2$ have to intersect. By \Cref{R: EKR for n=2k}, there are at most $\Gauss{2n-1}{n-1}$ such spaces.

    In conclusion, there are $\Gauss{n}{1}$ points in $A$ and for every point $P$ in $A$ there are at most $\Gauss{2n-1}{n-1}$ many flags $(A',B')\in \mathcal{F}$ with distinct $n$-spaces, such that $A'\cap B=\emptyset$ and $B\cap B'=P$. Since $\Gauss{n}{1}\cdot \Gauss{2n-1}{n-1}$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n-1})\cdot \mathcal{O}(q^{(n-1)n})=\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})$ the statement follows.
nodes.statement_short: Flags with $A'$ skew to $B$ have $B'\cap B$ in $A$; for a fixed point $P$ their $B'$ pairwise meet in lines, so EKR in the quotient PG$(2n-1,q)$ bounds them.

nodes.name: Few red spaces imply small coclique
nodes.statement: Let $n\geq 3$ and let $\mathcal{F}$ be a maximal coclique of $\Gamma_{2n}$ such that the number of red spaces in $\mathcal{F}$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-2})$. Then $|\mathcal{F}|$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2+n-2})$.
assumptions: Let $n\geq 3$
let $\mathcal{F}$ be a maximal coclique of $\Gamma_{2n}$ such that the number of red spaces in $\mathcal{F}$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-2})$.
conclusions: Then $|\mathcal{F}|$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2+n-2})$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.5
nodes.statement:
The number of red spaces is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-2})$ and a red space is contained in $\Gauss{n+1}{1}$ flags of $\mathcal{F}$, hence the number of flags in $\mathcal{F}$ that contain a red space is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-2})\cdot \Gauss{n+1}{1}=\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2+n-2})$. 
   
   We show that the number of flags in $\mathcal{F}$ with a yellow space is also $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2+n-2})$. Assume that this is not the case.

     By \Cref{L: many yellow pw skew}, there are $n+1$ pairwise skew yellow $(n-1)$-spaces, or $n+1$ yellow $n$-spaces in pairwise general position in $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$. We assume that $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$ contains $n+1$ pairwise skew $(n-1)$-spaces $A_1,\ldots,A_{n+1}$ and show that the number of flags in $\mathcal{F}$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2+n-2})$, for yellow $n$-spaces dual arguments suffice.
     
     Let $1\leq i\leq n+1$. 
     Any flag $(A,B)\in \mathcal{F}$ satisfies $B\cap A_i=\emptyset$ or $B\cap A_i\neq\emptyset$.
     By the dual statement of \Cref{L: yellows meet almost all}, the number of flags $(A,B)\in \mathcal{F}$ with distinct $(n-1)$-spaces and with $A_i\cap B=\emptyset$ is at most $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})$. As the red spaces are already accounted for, we can safely assume that these $(n-1)$-spaces are all yellow. This yields that the number of flags $(A,B)\in \mathcal{F}$ with $A_i\cap B=\emptyset$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})\Gauss{n}{1}=\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2+n-2})$. 
     
     Hence, the number of flags $(A,B)\in \mathcal{F}$ with $A_i\cap B=\emptyset$ for some $1\leq i\leq n+1$ is $(n+1)\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2+n-2})=\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2+n-2})$. All other flags in $\mathcal{F}$ must have an $n$-space that meets $A_1,\ldots,A_{n+1}$. By \Cref{L: few that meet all}, the number of $n$-spaces that meet $A_1,\ldots,A_{n+1}$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})$. As the red spaces are already accounted for, we can safely assume that these $n$-spaces are all yellow. This yields that the number of flags $(A,B)\in \mathcal{F}$ with $A_i\cap B\neq\emptyset$ for all $1\leq i\leq n+1$  is also $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})\Gauss{n}{1}=\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2+n-2})$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume many flags on yellow spaces; take $n+1$ pairwise skew yellow $(n-1)$-spaces (Lemma 4.2) and bound flags missing some $A_i$ (Lemma 4.4) and flags meeting all (Lemma 4.3).

nodes.name: Reduce to case (a)(i) by duality
nodes.statement: Now, we count the size of the set $\mathcal{F}$ as described in \Cref{E: main} $(a)(i)$ and remark that duality implies that all constructions described in \Cref{E: main} have the same size.

nodes.name: Count flags with $B\subseteq H$
nodes.statement: The number of $n$-spaces incident with a hyperplane $H$ of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$ is $\Gauss{2n}{n+1}$. Each such $n$-space contains exactly $\Gauss{n+1}{1}$ many $(n-1)$-spaces.

nodes.name: Count flags with $A$ through $X$ in $H$ and $B\not\subseteq H$
nodes.statement: The number of $(n-1)$-spaces incident with the point $X$ and the hyperplane $H$ is $\Gauss{2n-1}{n-1}$. Each such $(n-1)$-space is incident with exactly $q^n$ many $n$-spaces that are not contained in $H$.
nodes.statement_short: Count flags with $A$ through $X$ in $H$ and $B\not\subseteq H$

nodes.name: Recall the conditional chromatic number result
nodes.statement: In 2023 the chromatic number of $\Gamma_{2n}$ was determined modulo a conjecture by D'haeseleer, Metsch and Werner \cite{Jozefien_some}.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the conditional chromatic number result

nodes.name: Theorem 1.2 confirms the conjecture
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{T: main} is precisely the confirmation that their conjecture is true. Therefore, by proving Theorem \ref{T: main} we immediately get the following.

nodes.name: Full weight implies every $A'$ meets $B$
nodes.statement: First, assume that the number  of flags in $\mathcal{F}$ that contain $B$ is $\Gauss{n+1}{1}$. This means that for every $(n-1)$-space $A$ contained in $B$, we have $(A,B)\in \mathcal{F}$. Let $(A',B')$ be an $(n-1,n)$-flag of $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$ with $A'\cap B=\emptyset$. Then $B\cap B'$ is just a point $P$. There exist $(n-1)$-spaces in $B$ that are skew to $P$. Therefore, there are flags in $\mathcal{F}$ that are opposite to $(A',B')$, hence $(A',B')$ is not in $\mathcal{F}$.

nodes.name: Every $A'$ meets $B$ implies full weight by maximality
nodes.statement: Now, assume that every flag $(A',B')\in \mathcal{F}$ satisfies $A'\cap B\neq \emptyset$. Then every flag $(A,B)$, where $A$ is an $(n-1)$-space contained in $B$, is non-opposite to all flags in $\mathcal{F}$. By maximality of $\mathcal{F}$, all such flags are in $\mathcal{F}$. The number of flags in $\mathcal{F}$ containing $B$ is $\Gauss{n+1}{n}=\Gauss{n+1}{1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Every $A'$ meets $B$ implies full weight by maximality

nodes.name: Case of flags with $A'$ skew to $B$
nodes.statement: Finally, assume that there exist $(n-1,n)$-flags in $\mathcal{F}$ whose $(n-1)$-spaces are skew to $B$. Let $(A'_1,B'_1),\ldots,(A'_k,B'_k)$ be all these flags. Now, any flag $(A,B)\in \mathcal{F}$ has to satisfy $A\cap B'_1\neq\emptyset,\ldots, A\cap B'_k\neq\emptyset$.
nodes.statement_short: Case of flags with $A'$ skew to $B$

nodes.name: Define the points $P_i=B'_i\cap B$
nodes.statement:
Let $1\leq i\leq k$.
    As $A'_i\cap B=\emptyset$, we know that $B'_i\cap B$ is a point, say $P_i$.

nodes.name: $A$ must contain the span $S$
nodes.statement: Now $A$ has to be incident with all points $P_i$. In other words, the span of the points $P_i$ has to be incident with $A$. Let $s$ be the dimension of the span $S$ of the points $P_i$.

nodes.name: Bound $\dim S$
nodes.statement: We have $0\leq s\leq n-1$, otherwise there could be no flag in $\mathcal{F}$ that contains $B$.

nodes.name: Maximality gives $[n-s]_q$ flags
nodes.statement: By maximality of $\mathcal{F}$, any $(n-1)$-space $A$ that is incident with $S$ and $B$ occurs in a flag $(A,B)$ of $\mathcal{F}$. There are $\Gauss{n-s}{(n-1)-s}=\Gauss{n-s}{1}$ such flags.

nodes.name: Reduce to $n$-spaces by duality
nodes.statement: We only show the statement regarding $n$-spaces, the statement for $(n-1)$-spaces follows by duality.

nodes.name: Characterize red via Lemma 2.1
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{L: possible weights} an $n$-space $B$ is red if and only if every flag $(A',B')\in \mathcal{F}$ satisfies $A'\cap B\neq \emptyset$.

nodes.name: General position yields opposite flags
nodes.statement: If $B_1$ and $B_2$ are two $n$-spaces in general position, i.e. they intersect only in a point, then there exist $(n-1)$-spaces $A_1, A_2$ with $A_1\subseteq B_1$ and $A_2\subseteq B_2$, such that  $A_1\cap B_2=A_2\cap B_1=\emptyset$.

nodes.name: Assume many red $(n-1)$-spaces
nodes.statement: Assume that the number of red $(n-1)$-spaces in $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$ is not $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-2})$, then it is in particular $> \Gauss{2n}{n-1}-q^{n(n-1)}\Gauss{n}{1}$ for $n\geq 3$.

nodes.name: EKR/Hilton-Milner gives a common point $P$
nodes.statement: \Cref{R: EKR + HM vectorspaces} and \Cref{Remark 1} imply that there exists a point $P$, such that every red $(n-1)$-space is incident with $P$.

nodes.name: Each $B$ of $\mathcal{F}$ meets all red spaces
nodes.statement: By \Cref{C: possible weights}, for every flag $(A,B)\in \mathcal{F}$, we have that it's $n$-space meets all red $(n-1)$-spaces.
nodes.statement_short: Each $B$ of $\mathcal{F}$ meets all red spaces

nodes.name: An $n$-space missing $P$ meets too few red spaces
nodes.statement: Let $B$ be an $n$-space that intersects all red $(n-1)$-spaces with $P\notin B$. The number of lines that meet $P$ and $B$ is $\Gauss{n+1}{1}$, as this is the number of points in $B$. The number of $(n-1)$-subspaces incident with a line is $\Gauss{2n-1}{n-2}$. Therefore, there are at most $\Gauss{n+1}{1}\cdot \Gauss{2n-1}{n-2}$ red $(n-1)$-spaces in this case and this number is $\mathcal{O}(q^n)\cdot \mathcal{O}(q^{(n-2)(n+1)})=\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-2})$, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: An $n$-space missing $P$ meets too few red spaces

nodes.name: Every $(n-1)$-space through $P$ is red
nodes.statement: Hence, for all flags $(A,B)\in \mathcal{F}$, it's $n$-space meets $P$. By maximality of $\mathcal{F}$, every $(n-1)$-space incident with $P$ is red. For $n$-spaces the statement follows by duality.

nodes.name: Hyperplane $H$ of red $n$-spaces
nodes.statement: By \Cref{C: number of red spaces}, we know that there is a hyperplane $H$ such that every $n$-space incident with $H$ is red.

nodes.name: Every $A$ lies in $H$
nodes.statement: By \Cref{L: possible weights}, we have for any flag $(A,B)$ in $\mathcal{F}$ that $A$ intersects all the $n$-spaces in $H$. This is only possible if $A\subseteq H$.

nodes.name: Count flags inside $H$
nodes.statement: The number of flags $(A,B)$ with $A,B\subseteq H$ is $\Gauss{2n}{n+1} \Gauss{n+1}{n}=\Gauss{2n}{n-1} \Gauss{n+1}{1}$.

nodes.name: The $A$'s of flags outside $H$ pairwise meet
nodes.statement: Let $(A_1,B_1)$ and $(A_2,B_2)$ be flags of $\mathcal{F}$ with $B_1,B_2$ not red, i.e. $B_1,B_2$ are not contained in $H$. If $A_1$ and $A_2$ are skew, then $B_1$ is skew to $A_2$, as $B_1$ intersects $H$ only in $A_1$. Similarly $B_2$ is skew to $A_1$. So if $A_1$ and $A_2$ are skew, then the flags $(A_1,B_1)$ and $(A_2,B_2)$ are opposite, which is a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: The $A$'s of flags outside $H$ pairwise meet

nodes.name: Apply EKR/Hilton-Milner in $H$
nodes.statement: In conclusion the flags $(A,B)$ in $\mathcal{F}$ with $B\not\subseteq H$ have $(n-1)$-spaces that pairwise intersect in $H$. By \Cref{R: EKR for n=2k} there are two options. Either there is a point or $(2n-2)$-space in $H$ that is incident with $A$ for any such flag $(A,B)$, or there are at most $f(n,q)$ distinct $(n-1)$-subspaces $A$ in these flags.

nodes.name: Common point or $(2n-2)$-space: Example 1.1(a)
nodes.statement: If there is a point or $(2n-2)$-space in $H$ that is incident with $A$ for any flag $(A,B)$ with $B\not\subseteq H$, then $\mathcal{F}$ is as in Example \ref{E: main} (a).

nodes.name: Otherwise the $f(n,q)$ bound
nodes.statement: If no such point or $(2n-2)$-space exists, then we have $ \Gauss{2n}{n-1} \Gauss{n+1}{1}$ flags $(A,B)$ with $A,B\subseteq H$ and since any $(n-1)$-space in $H$ is incident with $q^n$ many $n$-spaces that are not contained in $H$, we have at most $q^n\cdot f(n,q)$ many flags $(A,B)$ with $B\not\subseteq H$. In conclusion, we have at most $\Gauss{2n}{n-1} \Gauss{n+1}{1} +f(n,q)\cdot q^n$ flags in this case.

nodes.name: Flags on red spaces are few
nodes.statement: The number of red spaces is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-2})$ and a red space is contained in $\Gauss{n+1}{1}$ flags of $\mathcal{F}$, hence the number of flags in $\mathcal{F}$ that contain a red space is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-2})\cdot \Gauss{n+1}{1}=\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2+n-2})$.
nodes.statement_short: Flags on red spaces are few

nodes.name: Assume $\mathcal{F}$ is large; then there are many yellow spaces
nodes.statement:
Let us assume that $|\mathcal{F}|$ is not $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2+n-2})$. 
    As a yellow space is contained in at most $\Gauss{n}{1}$ flags of $\mathcal{F}$, the number of yellow spaces cannot be $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $\mathcal{F}$ is large; then there are many yellow spaces

nodes.name: Erdős-Matching bound contradicts
nodes.statement: If there are at most $n$ yellow $(n-1)$-spaces in $\mathcal{F}$ that are pairwise skew, \Cref{R: EM for vector spaces} implies that the number of yellow $(n-1)$-spaces is at most $n \Gauss{2n}{n-1}$ which is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})$.

nodes.name: Dual case
nodes.statement: For yellow $n$-spaces the result follows by duality.

nodes.name: Introduce $P_i=B\cap A_i$
nodes.statement:
Let $B$ be an $n$-space that meets $A_1,\ldots,A_{n+1}$. 
     Then $B\cap A_i$ has to be some subspace $P_i$ for all $1\leq i\leq n+1$.

nodes.name: Counting strategy
nodes.statement: First, we will count subspaces $P_i$ in $A_i$ (for $i$ in a subset of $\{1,\ldots,n+1\}$) and then we will consider all $n$-spaces incident with the span of the $P_i$. This gives an upper bound on the number of $n$-spaces that meet $A_1,\ldots,A_{n+1}$.

nodes.name: Fix the dimensions $s_i$
nodes.statement: As a first step, we can choose dimensions $s_1,\ldots,s_{n+1}$, where $s_i=dim(P_i)$. As $0\leq s_i\leq n-1$, there are $n$ options for every $i$, so in total at most $n^{n+1}$ options. From now on, we assume that $s_1,\ldots,s_{n+1}$ are fixed.

nodes.name: Two cases on partial spans
nodes.statement: We distinguish two cases: Either we choose $P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1}$ in such a way that there is an $i$, such that the span $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i'} \rangle$ meets $A_{i'+1}$, or we choose $P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1}$ such that there is no such $i'$.

nodes.name: Case 1: some partial span meets the next $A$
nodes.statement:
\textbf{\underline{Case 1:}} We choose $P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1}$, such that there exists an $i'\in \{2,\ldots,n\}$, with the property that the span $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i'} \rangle$ meets $A_{i'+1}$. Let $i$ be the smallest integer with this property.\\

This implies that $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$ does not meet $A_i$, hence $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$ is skew to $P_i$. Furthermore, $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-2} \rangle$ does not meet $A_{i-1}$, hence $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-2} \rangle$ is skew to $P_{i-1}$, so $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-2} \rangle$, $P_{i-1}$ and $P_i$ are pairwise skew. Using the same argument $i-1$ times yields that $P_1,\ldots,P_i$ are pairwise skew.

In particular, we have
\begin{align} \begin{split}
    dim(\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i} \rangle)&=dim( P_1)+\ldots+dim(P_i)+(i-1)\\
    &= s_1+\ldots+s_i+(i-1)   
\end{split}
\end{align}
and
\begin{align} dim(\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle)=s_1+\ldots+s_{i-1}+(i-2). 
\end{align}
For any $j\leq i-1$ the number of $s_j$-subspaces in $A_j$ is $\Gauss{n}{s_j+1}$.
 As $P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1}$ are pairwise skew, the number of distinct subspaces $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$ is bound by the number of tuples $( P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1})$. So, the number of subspaces $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$ is at most
 $\Gauss{n}{s_1+1} \ldots   \Gauss{n}{s_{i-1}+1}$.

For any subspace $P_i$ skew to $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$, we have that $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1},P_i \rangle=\langle \langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle,P_i \rangle$ consists of all points that are on a line $g$ that intersects $P_i$ and $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$.\\
 Let $Q_1$ be a point in  $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$. As $Q_1$ is in  $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$, which is skew to the $(n-1)$-space $A_i$, the span $S$ of $Q_1$ and $A_i$ has dimension $n$. If we assume that $S$ meets $A_{i+1}$ in at least a line, then $A_i$ (which has codimension $1$ in $S$) would meet $A_{i+1}$, which is a contradiction. 
 So, $S$ meets $A_{i+1}$ in at most a point $Q_3$. If such a point $Q_3$ exists, then the line $Q_1Q_3$ intersects $P_i$ in a point.
In other words: For every point $Q_1$ in $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$ there is at most one point $Q_2$ in $A_i$ with the property that $Q_1Q_2$ intersects $A_{i+1}$.
 Recall from (\ref{A: dim P_1,...,P_i-1}) that $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1}\rangle$ has dimension $s_1+\ldots+s_{i-1}+(i-2)$.
 Therefore, $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1}\rangle$ contains exactly $\Gauss{s_1+\ldots+s_{i-1}+ (i-1)}{1}$ many points $Q_1$.
Hence, the number of points $Q_2$ in $A_i$, with the property that there is a $Q_1$ in $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1}\rangle$ such that $Q_1Q_2$ intersects $A_{i+1}$, is at most  $\Gauss{s_1+\ldots+s_{i-1}+ (i-1)}{1}$. \\
As $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i} \rangle$ meets $A_{i+1}$, we have that $P_i$ is an $s_i$-subspaces in $A_i$ that is incident with one such point $Q_2$. The number of $s_i$-subspaces in $A_i$ incident with a fixed point is $\Gauss{n-1}{s_i}$.
 So, if $P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1}$ are fixed, there are at most $\Gauss{s_1+\ldots+s_{i-1}+ (i-1)}{1}\Gauss{n-1}{s_i}$ options for $P_i$. \\ 
Recall from (\ref{A: dim P_1,...,P_i}) that $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i} \rangle$ has dimension $(s_1+\ldots+s_i+i-1)$.
Therefore, the number of $n$-spaces $B$ that contain  $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i} \rangle$ is at most
 $\Gauss{2n-(s_1+\ldots+s_i+i-1)}{n-(s_1+\ldots+s_i+i-1)}$.  
Any $n$-space that contains $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1} \rangle$, must also contain $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i} \rangle$. Hence, we have at most
    \begin{align*}
        &\Gauss{n}{s_1+1} \ldots   \Gauss{n}{s_{i-1}+1}  \cdot \Gauss{s_1+\ldots+s_{i-1}+i-1}{1}\Gauss{n-1}{s_i}   \cdot\Gauss{2n-(s_1+\ldots+s_i+i-1)}{n-(s_1+\ldots+s_i+i-1)}
    \end{align*}
   many $n$-subspaces $B$ in Case 1. This number is a $q$-polynomial of degree at most
\begin{align*}
    &\left( \sum\limits_{j=1}^{i-1}(s_j+1)(n-s_j-1) \right)
    +(i-2+\sum\limits_{j=1}^{i-1}s_j)+s_i(n-1-s_i)+(n-i+1-\sum\limits_{j=1}^{i}s_j)n\\
    &=n^2 -\sum\limits_{j=1}^{i}(s_j^2+s_j) - 1\leq n^2-1.
\end{align*}

This implies that in this case the number in question is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Case 1: some partial span meets the next $A$

nodes.name: Case 2: no partial span meets the next $A$
nodes.statement:
\textbf{\underline{Case 2:}} We choose $P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1}$, such that there exists  no $i'\in \{2,\ldots,n\}$, with the property that the span $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i'} \rangle$ meets $A_{i'+1}$. \\

We start with the same argument as in Case 1. 
The span $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{n} \rangle$ does not meet $A_{n+1}$, hence $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{n} \rangle$ is skew to $P_{n+1}$. 
Furthermore, $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{n-1} \rangle$ does not meet $A_{n}$, hence $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{n-1} \rangle$ is skew to $P_{n}$, so $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{n-1} \rangle$, $P_{n}$ and $P_{n+1}$ are pairwise skew. 
Using the same argument $n$ times yields that $P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1}$ are pairwise skew. Hence, 
$\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1}\rangle$ has dimension $s_1+\ldots+s_{n+1}+n$.\\
Let $B$ be an $n$-space that contains $P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1}$.
As $B$ has dimension $n$, we have $s_1+\ldots+s_{n+1}+n\leq n$, hence $s_i=0$ for all $1\leq i\leq n+1$ and every subspace $P_i$ is a point. In particular, $B$ is the span of all points $P_i$. There are $\Gauss{n}{1}$ points in every $(n-1)$-space $A_i$, hence there are at most $\Gauss{n}{1}^{n+1}$ many $n$-spaces $B$ that are equal to $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1} \rangle$ and this number is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Case 2: no partial span meets the next $A$

nodes.name: Both cases give $O(q^{n^2-1})$
nodes.statement: In conclusion we see that in both cases the number in question is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})$.

nodes.name: Choose the smallest index $i$
nodes.statement: \textbf{\underline{Case 1:}} We choose $P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1}$, such that there exists an $i'\in \{2,\ldots,n\}$, with the property that the span $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i'} \rangle$ meets $A_{i'+1}$. Let $i$ be the smallest integer with this property.

nodes.name: $P_1,\ldots,P_i$ are pairwise skew
nodes.statement: This implies that $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$ does not meet $A_i$, hence $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$ is skew to $P_i$. Furthermore, $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-2} \rangle$ does not meet $A_{i-1}$, hence $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-2} \rangle$ is skew to $P_{i-1}$, so $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-2} \rangle$, $P_{i-1}$ and $P_i$ are pairwise skew.

nodes.name: Dimensions of the partial spans
Count the spans $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1}\rangle$
nodes.statement:
For any $j\leq i-1$ the number of $s_j$-subspaces in $A_j$ is $\Gauss{n}{s_j+1}$.
 As $P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1}$ are pairwise skew, the number of distinct subspaces $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$ is bound by the number of tuples $( P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1})$. So, the number of subspaces $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$ is at most
 $\Gauss{n}{s_1+1} \ldots   \Gauss{n}{s_{i-1}+1}$.

nodes.name: Each $Q_1$ determines at most one $Q_2$
nodes.statement:
For any subspace $P_i$ skew to $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$, we have that $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1},P_i \rangle=\langle \langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle,P_i \rangle$ consists of all points that are on a line $g$ that intersects $P_i$ and $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$.\\
 Let $Q_1$ be a point in  $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$. As $Q_1$ is in  $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$, which is skew to the $(n-1)$-space $A_i$, the span $S$ of $Q_1$ and $A_i$ has dimension $n$. If we assume that $S$ meets $A_{i+1}$ in at least a line, then $A_i$ (which has codimension $1$ in $S$) would meet $A_{i+1}$, which is a contradiction. 
 So, $S$ meets $A_{i+1}$ in at most a point $Q_3$. If such a point $Q_3$ exists, then the line $Q_1Q_3$ intersects $P_i$ in a point.
In other words: For every point $Q_1$ in $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1} \rangle$ there is at most one point $Q_2$ in $A_i$ with the property that $Q_1Q_2$ intersects $A_{i+1}$.

nodes.name: Recall dimension (2)
nodes.statement: Recall from (\ref{A: dim P_1,...,P_i-1}) that $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1}\rangle$ has dimension $s_1+\ldots+s_{i-1}+(i-2)$.

nodes.name: Bound the number of points $Q_2$
nodes.statement:
Therefore, $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1}\rangle$ contains exactly $\Gauss{s_1+\ldots+s_{i-1}+ (i-1)}{1}$ many points $Q_1$.
Hence, the number of points $Q_2$ in $A_i$, with the property that there is a $Q_1$ in $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1}\rangle$ such that $Q_1Q_2$ intersects $A_{i+1}$, is at most  $\Gauss{s_1+\ldots+s_{i-1}+ (i-1)}{1}$. \\

nodes.name: Bound the choices of $P_i$
nodes.statement:
As $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i} \rangle$ meets $A_{i+1}$, we have that $P_i$ is an $s_i$-subspaces in $A_i$ that is incident with one such point $Q_2$. The number of $s_i$-subspaces in $A_i$ incident with a fixed point is $\Gauss{n-1}{s_i}$.
 So, if $P_1,\ldots,P_{i-1}$ are fixed, there are at most $\Gauss{s_1+\ldots+s_{i-1}+ (i-1)}{1}\Gauss{n-1}{s_i}$ options for $P_i$.

nodes.name: Recall dimension (1)
nodes.statement: Recall from (\ref{A: dim P_1,...,P_i}) that $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i} \rangle$ has dimension $(s_1+\ldots+s_i+i-1)$.

nodes.name: Total count in Case 1
Degree is at most $n^2-1$
Case 1 gives $O(q^{n^2-1})$
nodes.statement: This implies that in this case the number in question is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})$.

nodes.name: Case 2 hypothesis
nodes.statement:
\textbf{\underline{Case 2:}} We choose $P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1}$, such that there exists  no $i'\in \{2,\ldots,n\}$, with the property that the span $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{i'} \rangle$ meets $A_{i'+1}$. \\

We start with the same argument as in Case 1.

nodes.name: $P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1}$ pairwise skew; dimension of their span
nodes.statement:
The span $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{n} \rangle$ does not meet $A_{n+1}$, hence $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{n} \rangle$ is skew to $P_{n+1}$. 
Furthermore, $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{n-1} \rangle$ does not meet $A_{n}$, hence $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{n-1} \rangle$ is skew to $P_{n}$, so $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{n-1} \rangle$, $P_{n}$ and $P_{n+1}$ are pairwise skew. 
Using the same argument $n$ times yields that $P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1}$ are pairwise skew. Hence, 
$\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1}\rangle$ has dimension $s_1+\ldots+s_{n+1}+n$.
nodes.statement_short: $P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1}$ pairwise skew; dimension of their span

nodes.name: All $P_i$ are points spanning $B$
nodes.statement:
Let $B$ be an $n$-space that contains $P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1}$.
As $B$ has dimension $n$, we have $s_1+\ldots+s_{n+1}+n\leq n$, hence $s_i=0$ for all $1\leq i\leq n+1$ and every subspace $P_i$ is a point. In particular, $B$ is the span of all points $P_i$.

nodes.name: Count the spans: $O(q^{n^2-1})$
nodes.statement: There are $\Gauss{n}{1}$ points in every $(n-1)$-space $A_i$, hence there are at most $\Gauss{n}{1}^{n+1}$ many $n$-spaces $B$ that are equal to $\langle P_1,\ldots,P_{n+1} \rangle$ and this number is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})$.

nodes.name: $B'\cap B$ lies in $A$
nodes.statement: Since $B$ is a yellow $n$-space there exists an $(n-1)$-space $A$, such that $(A,B)\in \mathcal{F}$. Therefore, any flag $(A',B')\in \mathcal{F}$ with $A'\cap B=\emptyset$ has to satisfy that the point $B'\cap B$ is in  $A$.

nodes.name: Flags through the same point have $B'$ meeting in a line
nodes.statement:
Consider two flags $(A'_1,B'_1),(A'_2,B'_2)\in \mathcal{F}$ with $A'_1\cap B=\emptyset$ and $A'_2\cap B=\emptyset$ and assume $B'_1\cap B=B'_2\cap B=P$.
    If $B'_1\cap B'_2=P$, then $A'_1\cap B'_2=\emptyset=A'_2\cap B'_1$ as $A'_1$ and $A'_2$ are skew to $B$. Then the flags $(A'_1,B'_1),(A'_2,B'_2)$ are opposite, which is a contradiction. Therefore, the $n$-spaces $B'_1$ and $B'_2$ have to meet in at least a line containing $P$.
nodes.statement_short: Flags through the same point have $B'$ meeting in a line

nodes.name: EKR in the quotient PG$(2n-1,q)$
nodes.statement: In the quotient space of $P$, which has dimension $2n-1$, this means that the $(n-1)$-spaces corresponding to $B'_1$ and $B'_2$ have to intersect. By \Cref{R: EKR for n=2k}, there are at most $\Gauss{2n-1}{n-1}$ such spaces.

nodes.name: Sum over the points of $A$
nodes.statement: In conclusion, there are $\Gauss{n}{1}$ points in $A$ and for every point $P$ in $A$ there are at most $\Gauss{2n-1}{n-1}$ many flags $(A',B')\in \mathcal{F}$ with distinct $n$-spaces, such that $A'\cap B=\emptyset$ and $B\cap B'=P$. Since $\Gauss{n}{1}\cdot \Gauss{2n-1}{n-1}$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n-1})\cdot \mathcal{O}(q^{(n-1)n})=\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})$ the statement follows.

nodes.name: Flags on red spaces are few
nodes.statement: The number of red spaces is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-2})$ and a red space is contained in $\Gauss{n+1}{1}$ flags of $\mathcal{F}$, hence the number of flags in $\mathcal{F}$ that contain a red space is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-2})\cdot \Gauss{n+1}{1}=\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2+n-2})$.
nodes.statement_short: Flags on red spaces are few

nodes.name: Assume many flags on yellow spaces
nodes.statement: We show that the number of flags in $\mathcal{F}$ with a yellow space is also $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2+n-2})$. Assume that this is not the case.
nodes.statement_short: Assume many flags on yellow spaces

nodes.name: Obtain $n+1$ pairwise skew yellow spaces
nodes.statement: By \Cref{L: many yellow pw skew}, there are $n+1$ pairwise skew yellow $(n-1)$-spaces, or $n+1$ yellow $n$-spaces in pairwise general position in $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$. We assume that $\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)$ contains $n+1$ pairwise skew $(n-1)$-spaces $A_1,\ldots,A_{n+1}$ and show that the number of flags in $\mathcal{F}$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2+n-2})$, for yellow $n$-spaces dual arguments suffice.

nodes.name: Flags with $B$ skew to $A_i$ are few (dual Lemma 4.4)
nodes.statement:
Let $1\leq i\leq n+1$. 
     Any flag $(A,B)\in \mathcal{F}$ satisfies $B\cap A_i=\emptyset$ or $B\cap A_i\neq\emptyset$.
     By the dual statement of \Cref{L: yellows meet almost all}, the number of flags $(A,B)\in \mathcal{F}$ with distinct $(n-1)$-spaces and with $A_i\cap B=\emptyset$ is at most $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})$. As the red spaces are already accounted for, we can safely assume that these $(n-1)$-spaces are all yellow. This yields that the number of flags $(A,B)\in \mathcal{F}$ with $A_i\cap B=\emptyset$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})\Gauss{n}{1}=\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2+n-2})$.
nodes.statement_short: Flags with $B$ skew to $A_i$ are few (dual Lemma 4.4)

nodes.name: Union over $i$
nodes.statement: Hence, the number of flags $(A,B)\in \mathcal{F}$ with $A_i\cap B=\emptyset$ for some $1\leq i\leq n+1$ is $(n+1)\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2+n-2})=\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2+n-2})$.

nodes.name: Flags meeting all $A_i$ are few (Lemma 4.3)
nodes.statement: All other flags in $\mathcal{F}$ must have an $n$-space that meets $A_1,\ldots,A_{n+1}$. By \Cref{L: few that meet all}, the number of $n$-spaces that meet $A_1,\ldots,A_{n+1}$ is $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})$. As the red spaces are already accounted for, we can safely assume that these $n$-spaces are all yellow. This yields that the number of flags $(A,B)\in \mathcal{F}$ with $A_i\cap B\neq\emptyset$ for all $1\leq i\leq n+1$  is also $\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2-1})\Gauss{n}{1}=\mathcal{O}(q^{n^2+n-2})$.
